readerTitle: Toblerone made the gaps wider, and everyone noticed
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Mondelez의 Toblerone, 2016년 영국 중량 축소와 2018년 복원) + 가상 적용 (소프트웨어 구독 서비스)
insight: 숨긴 가격 인상은 들키는 순간 공개적인 가격 인상보다 더 큰 신뢰 비용을 낸다. 제품의 상징을 건드리는 축소는 반드시 들킨다.
misconception: 가격을 그대로 두고 양을 줄이면 고객은 모르거나 덜 신경 쓴다. 그래서 가격 인상보다 안전하다.

sources.text: BBC News (2016년 11월), Toblerone 영국 제품의 중량 축소(400g→360g, 170g→150g)와 봉우리 간격 확대 보도
The Guardian (2016년 11월), Mondelez가 원재료 비용 상승을 이유로 든 해명 보도
BBC News (2018년 7월), Toblerone 영국 제품이 원래 모양과 중량으로 돌아오고 가격이 오른다는 보도

factChecks.note: 2016년 11월 영국에서 400g 바가 360g, 170g 바가 150g으로 줄고 봉우리 사이 간격이 넓어졌다는 내용을 BBC·Guardian 원문으로 다시 확인하세요. 400→360은 10% 감소입니다.
Mondelez는 원재료 비용 상승을 이유로 들었고 브렉시트 때문은 아니라고 밝혔다는 보도가 있습니다. 카드에는 '여러 원재료 비용 상승'으로만 적었습니다.
2018년 복원은 원래 중량으로 돌아오면서 가격이 올랐다는 보도입니다. 구체적인 가격(파운드)은 확실하지 않아 카드에 수치를 쓰지 않고 'at a higher price'로만 적었습니다.
축소가 처음 적용된 시장(영국 중심)과 다른 나라 포함 여부는 자료마다 표현이 다릅니다. 카드에는 'in the UK'로만 적었습니다.
소프트웨어 사례(카드 8)는 가상 사례이며 수치를 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Toblerone made the gaps wider, and everyone noticed
body: In late 2016, Toblerone bars in the UK changed shape. The famous chocolate peaks were still there, but the spaces between them got much wider.
The price stayed the same. The chocolate didn't. Within days, shoppers were posting side-by-side photos.

image.label: Two triangular chocolate bars, one with wide gaps between peaks
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 삼각형 봉우리 초콜릿 바 두 개를 나란히 배치. 위쪽은 봉우리가 촘촘하고, 아래쪽은 봉우리 사이가 눈에 띄게 넓음. 실제 Toblerone 로고, 포장 디자인, 마터호른 그림은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Your ingredient costs just went up.
body: You make a famous chocolate bar. Its shape is instantly recognizable. The cost of several ingredients has risen, and your margin per bar is shrinking.
Retailers and shoppers are used to the current price. What do you do?

options.text: Raise the price and keep the bar exactly as it is
options.feedback: Some shoppers will grumble and a few will buy less. But the change is honest and visible, so it doesn't feel like a trick.

options.text: Keep the price and make the bar lighter by spacing out the peaks
options.feedback: No sticker shock at the shelf. But you've changed the one thing everyone knows about your product, so the cut is easy to spot.

options.text: Keep the price and quietly make the bar a little shorter
options.feedback: Less obvious than wider gaps, so it may go unnoticed longer. If it's found, it still reads as a hidden price rise.

cards.title: Mondelez chose the gaps.
body: Toblerone's owner, Mondelez, cut the UK 400g bar to 360g and the 170g bar to 150g. It did this by widening the spaces between the peaks. Prices stayed put.

The company said rising costs for many ingredients forced the change. That was likely true. But the reason barely mattered. People saw a product they loved being made smaller **while they weren't supposed to notice**.

image.label: Weight labels: 400g crossed out, 360g beside it
image.brief: 단순한 인포그래픽. 초콜릿 바 실루엣 위에 "400g"에 취소선, 옆에 "360g". 아래에 "Same price" 라벨. 실제 상표와 포장은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Two years later, the peaks came back.
body: The new shape was mocked in newspapers and across social media. For many shoppers it became the textbook example of a hidden price rise.

In 2018, Mondelez announced that UK bars would return to their original shape and weight. They came back **at a higher price**. In the end, the company raised the price openly anyway, after paying for two years of bad press first.

cards.title: Shrinkflation meets perceived fairness
body: **Shrinkflation** means giving customers less for the same price. It is a price increase that doesn't show up on the price tag.

Customers judge price changes by more than the numbers. They ask whether the change feels **fair**. A cost-driven price rise usually feels acceptable. A cut that seems designed to slip past them feels like deception, and deception costs trust, not just sales.

cards.title: The cut hit the product's signature.
body: Shrinkflation tends to stay quiet only under certain conditions:
list: The change is small compared with the pack
Customers don't know the product's exact size
Nothing about the shape or look changes
Competitors make similar changes at the same time
cards.callout: Toblerone broke the third rule. Its shape *is* the brand, so the cut was visible the moment someone unwrapped a bar.

cards.title: A smaller pack isn't always a trick.
body: Costs do rise, and an open price increase still loses some customers. Shrinking a product can be reasonable when it's done in the open: a new, clearly labeled size, a lower price for a smaller pack, or a choice of both.
The problem isn't size. It's surprise. If you'd be embarrassed when customers discover the change, they will likely feel misled when they do.

cards.title: Now it's a software subscription.
body: You run a file-sharing app for small teams. Your hosting costs have risen. Your main plan includes a storage limit that customers rarely check.
How do you protect your margin?

options.text: Quietly lower the storage limit on the existing plan
options.feedback: The price looks stable, but users who hit the new limit will feel tricked. In software, a surprise limit often shows up mid-project, which makes it worse.

options.text: Raise the price with advance notice and explain the cost change
options.feedback: You'll lose a few price-sensitive users. You keep your reputation, and customers can plan around the change.

options.text: Keep current users as they are and launch a new plan with less storage
options.feedback: Fair to existing users and clearly labeled for new ones. It can work, but it adds plans to manage and still needs to be explained clearly.

cards.title: A hidden price rise is still a price rise, plus a trust bill.
body: Customers forgive costs going up. They are less forgiving when they feel tricked. Toblerone ended up raising its price anyway.
**Try it today:** list any recent change that gave customers a bit less for the same price. Would you be comfortable announcing it? If not, announce it, or change it.
